utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we will continue with the examination of the present witness, the Chamber received an application for a subpoena and is a bit concerned about whether this would work at all for the 30th of June or the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, basically the situation is as far as I understand it is the witness initially indicated that you he would not require a subpoena to appear and, I believe, on Monday, while I was in court, the witness was contacted again about making arrangements and then indicated that he would not appear voluntarily. So as a result, we filed the application for a subpoena yesterday. In terms of the logistics involved, I am reasonably -- first of all, no visa is required because the person is a citizen of Croatia. Secondly, that I believe a passport can be issued rather quickly, so I'm not sure -- I think the matter is -- depends upon how fast the Registry can issue the subpoena upon the Croatian authorities. So that I think is the crucial factor involved once the subpoena is served on the Croatian authority, I believe probably about three days to serve the witness and make appropriate arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The minimum is ten days. Usually it is impossible to do any quicker. Now, I do notice here that apparently there's no travel documents yet. Of course, you can apply for it, but, of course, you could have applied for it ten days or a month ago as well, at least the time you asked the witness to appear. So, therefore, whether it's realistic because I do understand that there were some health problems as well, which usually takes up more time. And is it true, but I just went through it very quickly, do we have date of birth, address? Do we have all the personnel data?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd have to check Mr. President. I don't have it in front of me right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, for us to issue a subpoena we would need such data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is not going to be a problem. If it is not in the subpoena you will have it by the first break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And have you considered alternatives? 92 bis, 92 ter -- no, of course, 92 doesn't work, videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We would be willing to do a videolink as with the witness. However, that's something, as I indicated to you a moment ago, this is all arisen rather quickly, so I will consult with the Prosecution and see first if they have any objection to a videolink and then if not, it is certainly something that we would consider in an effort to make sure that things proceed as scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, if we are supposed to issue a subpoena very quickly, then, of course, we would need to know from the Prosecution very quickly whether there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection regarding videolink, Mr. President or objection to the subpoena in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we're dealing with all of it, of course, the application at this moment is for a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There's no objection to the subpoena motion, Mr. President. However, for the videolink, if I could have a few moments this morning to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Misetic can do everything after the first break, so I take it that Prosecution would not -- in a competitive mood. I want to be serious. I mean, what the Chamber is trying to do at this moment is to see whether no time will be lost and whether we can resolve practical problems, and this is, of course, not to say that the Prosecution has one hour to respond to motions. Mr. Russo, at the same time, I do understand from your answer that you are responding in a similar mood; that is, to see whether we can resolve matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, one of the other options would be to take a bit more time in scheduling for this witness and see whether you can replace this witness but a less problematic witness at least as far as coming to The Hague is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because this is a risk that if we proceed we might be able to do it if everything goes right. If, however, we would not have the witness here on the 30th of June or the 1st of July and if we would lose another day, that is not something --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We will do -- certainly that is also an option we will consider, if there is a problem either with the videolink potentially, or the subpoena. What I can tell the Chamber is there is a specifically order we wish to call these witnesses, following this series of witnesses, the Chamber will hear from the prosecuting authority in these cases, and we believe that it has more value to the Chamber to be able to first hear the underlying crime base and then to be able to hear the testimony of the authorities that were involved in prosecuting the case and for that reason I think we would prefer not to go out of sequence [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would result in losing court days, then the Chamber might order you to give priority to not losing time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that also during the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, you're ready to continue the examination of Mr. Milas. Could Mr. Milas be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile I express the appreciation of the Chamber for the parties having been able to resolve the matter which still kept them apart yesterday. That's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had a late start; we had to deal with a procedural matter first. Our apologies for that. Mr. Milas, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday, and Mr. Misetic will now continue his examination. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, picking where we left off yesterday regarding the meeting on the 3rd of August, where Mr. Juric and Mr. Glavan were present. Can you tell the Chamber what your understanding was of what your chain of command above you would be --

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you still do not receive interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We were speaking yesterday of the meeting on 3rd of August where Mr. Juric and Mr. Glavan were present. My question is: If could you tell the Chamber what your understanding was after that meeting of what your chain of command was, starting with you and going above you. Who was in your chain of command?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, as far as the professional aspect of the crime police, military police is concerned, the chief, Ante Glavan, as an employee and member of the military police administration was in a certain sense my superior. He coordinated the work with the police administration in Zadar and Sibenik, but most of this, it must be said, was within the context of the civilian crime police and the work in reception centres. The next in the chain of command, the superior to Glavan, was, as far as I understood it, Major Ivan Juric who also received -- who received his orders from General Lausic. As of the 2nd of August, he was also the superior to the commander of the 72nd abdomen 73rd Battalions but only in that respect when -- only where members of the 72nd Battalion participated in the work of the 73rd so not of the entire 73rd. After the meeting, once Mr. Juric presented the order that he had received from General Lausic, and Ante Glavan also talked about what the work of the members of the crime police would be, in keeping -- pursuant to the order of General Lausic, with respect to the work that had to do done in the reception centre and also in the -- and also in the ambit of work of members of the crime police and their police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would that ambit of work include crimes committed by HV personnel?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did include that aspect of work, because, for instance, already on the 5th of August, in the morning, Major Juric held a meeting and he called Senior Lieutenant Glavan, Mr. Cicvaric, and me to these meetings, and he instructed us to visit the companies in Zadar and Sibenik and inspect the crime aspect of their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First of all, could you tell us how often -- first of all, could you tell us who you would sent your reports to during and after Operation Storm. First, let's focus on during Operation Storm. Who did you send written reports to?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily sometimes it would be in oral form and sometimes the reports would be written, and they would be daily reports, which would be sent to the operative duty service of the 72nd Battalion and the regular daily reports, if there were any activities, would be forward to the chief of the department of the crime -- military police crime investigation department within the military police administration. The other channel of information would be if there was any crime investigation conducted, and if that crime investigation resulted in a criminal report, the work done by the KVP would also be within the authority of the competent military court. If the military court issued an order to the crime -- to the military police crime CIB, they would also send their report to the military court, so this would be -- these would be the lines of communication and lines of reporting on the work of the military police crime investigation department. And at times, if the crime involved was a major violation of discipline or if they were crimes concerned, then General Lausic might request to receive direct information on how the investigation into those incidents was proceeding. Those cases were not very common, but they did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned regular reports in your answer. Where would extraordinary reports be sent?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sent the same way. The chief of the department of the military police crime investigation department at the request of General Lausic, the chief of the administration would send to him, but a criminal report would not be submitted every time. Rather, there would be interim reports on incidents that involved crimes, violent crimes, or major violations of discipline, military discipline, and if there was suspicion that a crime had been committed, they would also ask us to perform additional investigations but reports on that we would send exclusively to the chief of the department of the military police crime investigation department within the military police administration and if, so required, also to the chief of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we're missing something in your answer on the transcript. So let me ask you a broader question and hopefully you will restate it, what you said. Can you tell us what the role of the military prosecutor was that you were discussing in your prior answer?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the military prosecutor in Split, who also had his deputies in Zadar, Sibenik, and Dubrovnik was the following: He was to undertake proceedings for all those offences that, based on the laws in effect, he was authorised to investigate. In other words, once the military police crime investigation department submitted a criminal report, the military prosecutor would then take actions within the -- that are within the ambit of his responsibilities. The military prosecutor would sometimes receive criminal reports either from a military or a civilian person in which case he would ask the military police crime investigation department to take additional steps and conduct additional investigative procedures, which was called a request to collect additional information, where he would set out what those actions and steps in investigation were to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, did you send reports to the command of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your report, did you send your reports to the command of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These reports, reports of this type that I have just mentioned in answering your question, were not sent to the command of the Military District, nor to the commander of the Military District, nor to the brigade commanders within the Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. From the beginning of Operation Storm, who were you receiving your orders from, or instructions?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was receiving them exclusively along my professional chain of command, which means from the chief of the department of the military police crime investigation department within the military police administration, and these were not orders, because they were actually issued along a professional chain of command, so they were more instructions to conduct certain actions. Or, it -- there would be requests to report on certain aspects of the work of the military police crime investigation department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milas, one of the issues in this case concerns the burning of property, and in your supplemental statement, at paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And this is Exhibit D1533. I'm sorry, paragraph 3 and paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You discuss the issue of burning. Can you tell us, first of all, as a general matter by about the 16th of August, what was your impression about the scope of the problem of burning of property? What is -- for example in paragraph 3 of your statement you say: "The total number of burnt homes does not lead me to the conclusion that this represented a widespread occurrence." What was your basis to state that you did not conclude that this was a widespread occurrence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question because clearly that statement is given in the context of a document which is shown to the witness in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would be happy to show him the document. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 3371, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is a document that you were shown during your witness interview. It's a memorandum from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan dated 16 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Discussing the events in Croatia as of that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 7 of Mr. Akashi's report, he writes to

utterances.speaker: MR. ANNAN THAT
utterances.text: "The arson campaign conducted by the Croatian, which has been under way in Sector South since 8 August, has accounted for an estimated 200 houses. Almost the entire towns of Kistanje, Djevrska and Otric have been torched. Many hectares of farmland have also been burned. UNCRO reported seeing dozens of slaughtered farm animals throughout the Sector." Now, as the chief of the crime prevention service, does that number, 200 houses as of 16th of August, correspond with what your knowledge was as of that time-period about the number of houses that had been burned since 8 August?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Sector South is a very large area. If I'm correct, the Croatian Army, in Operation Storm, if we take into account both Sector North and Sector South, liberated some 10.700 or 11.000 square kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question by Mr. Misetic was clear, whether the number of 200 burnt houses corresponds with your personal observation. Could you tell us whether that does or does not correspond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the areas where I operated, that would be approximately the right number. And in view of how large that area was, I did not find this to be a widespread phenomenon, and, yes, it did happen in Kistanje, Djevrska, and Otric, and some areas. Well, as far as I could see and those are areas where I did travel and based on what I could observe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now this report goes until 16th of August because that's the date. Did you see any houses being burned after that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 16 August, I did not travel so much in the newly liberated territories. I sent sometime also in Split, Zadar, and Dubrovnik, because I had to also inspect those areas as well, and not just Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did that change considerably on 16th of August? When did you start focussing your work to be performed in, as you said, Split, Zadar ... I mean, you said after the 16th, is it a coincidence that you apparently changed your touring habits on that same day, or did you already start on the 12th or the 13th, or the 10th to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to other areas, toured other areas earlier as well, before 16th and after 16th. But I think already in early September I spent a greater portion of my time in the area of responsibility of the 72nd Battalion in Split and Dubrovnik. But there were sometimes when I would tour, Split, Sibenik, and Knin all in one day because that was the only way one could work in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now during all your touring, and I'm asking you about Sector South, 200 houses was the estimate of what you saw of houses being burned during this whole period, including, early September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is more or less how I wanted to put it as well. I went through Kistanje on the 10th and 12th of August, with Mr. Glavan, Cicvaric, and Maduna. We were in the centre of town, and my impression was not that there were so many houses that were torched; some were, but not to a great extent. You could see some combat damage on the houses; hence, that was the impression I gained in the area that I moved around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an impression as to how many you would say, not that many, but that's an assessment which -- how many houses in Kistanje you saw which had clear signs of burning or being torched recently? Five, 10, 20, 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the centre of town where I was, there must have been four, five, or six houses for which it was clear to me what happened. There's a statue in that area, and they were all around that part of town. It was clear that that was not combat damage, and I believed them to have been torched. I also knew that due to shelling, houses can catch fire, but it didn't seem to me to be the case. In that part of the -- of Kistanje, there were five or six houses. That's what I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And other parts of Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was there, we went the other way. We didn't take the central road. And in that area, I didn't see anything in particular, perhaps one or two torched houses. That's what I can recall, given the time that has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So 10th to 12th of August, altogether from what you observed, well, let's say five to six in the centre, one or two outside, which makes a total under 10. Is that what you observed as far as Kistanje is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be it. In terms of what I saw. Perhaps two or three days later I was in Otric, and there I saw two or three houses that were torched. Then in the area of Drnis, and this is all tied to the exact periods when I travelled through those areas and the extent of what I could see, of course. The previous portion of my testimony had to do with Kistanje itself between the 10th and the 12th only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, sorry, I'm trying to find the factual basis for observations because paragraph 3, of course, is commenting on a report and -- Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am done with this exhibit so I would ask that it be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1534.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 of your supplemental statement, Mr. Milas, talks about -- you were asked why such a small number of criminal charges in general were filed as well as almost no charges for the crime of arson. And part of your answer said that one of the main tasks of the crime investigation military police, during and immediately after Operation Storm, was the crime processing of the enemy prisoners of war, and then you give some statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit 65 ter 625 on the screen, pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, first, while that is being pulled up, Mr. Milas, can you explain why it is that your work in August and - sorry - during and immediately after Operation Storm was focussed on the processing of enemy POWs?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lausic's order, I can't recall the date now, although I believe it to be the 3rd of August, stated that the workers of the crime military police had to take part in scene-of-crime processing and crime processing of the captured members of the Army of Republika Srpska. One of the focal tasks was that one, primarily because in order to screen for those persons for whom there was reasonable doubt of having committed a crime directed against the Republic of Croatia, by virtue of which they were supposed to be handed over for further processing by the competent judge. After being arrested, their movement was restricted. It was the obligation of the police, under such circumstances, that they should undertake all measures first and foremost to establish whether there are any grounds for reasonable doubt of crimes committed. If there are, that person needs to be handed over to the competent judge with the criminal report. If there are no grounds for that, that person needs to be released immediately. I believe there were a total of 550 members of enemy formations who were interviewed by employees of the military crime police. Out of that number, there were less than 200 or 180 who were handed over to the competent military judge because there were grounds to believe that they had committed a crime against the Republic of Croatia. In most cases, these crimes involved armed rebellion and participating in the activities of the enemy armed forces. That was one of the primary tasks of the crime military police employees. We did this together or in cooperation with workers of the civilian police and the security service. One of the reasons for that was certainly because those captured members of enemy formations could provide information on the remaining and hidden weapons stocks of the Army of Republika Srpska, as well as any possible terrorist groups that might carry out terrorist acts, as well as the knowledge they had about potential minefields in the liberated territories. We know that many Croatian Army members were wounded or killed because of such mines. These would be the basic reasons due to which we were busy with that on a daily basis and to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 of the English in this document, please. Could you tell us how many of your people, I believe yesterday you testified that you had 45 to 50 people, I think that's in your statement, at your disposal in the 72nd Crime Prevention Service. How many of those people were employed in the processing of enemy POWs?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If in Knin we had seven employees, out of the seven, four were operative, authorised to conduct interviews. Then, at least two of them would conduct such interviews in the area of Knin. From Split, there must have been two or three that were sent. From Sibenik, there was Mr. Simic, who I'm quite certain sent one or two employees. The same goes for Zadar. So out of the total number of people, there were at least two employees per area who had to work on that throughout the day in order to gather such information the way I explained. That would be the bear minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you look at the document on your screen, did these interviews take place in these reception centres? For example, the reception centre of Zadar?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Zadar, in Sibenik, As well as in Knin. Because pursuant to the order of the MP administration chief and the agreement reached prior to Operation Storm at the level of the minister of the interior and defence, those tasked with organizing and working in the reception centres for civilians were exclusively civilian policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you look at the page on the screen at paragraph 5.1, do those statistics -- are they consistent with your recollections as to roughly how many people were processed in the reception centre, Zadar?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be correct. On a daily basis, Major Glavan collected information. As of the 4th of August, and throughout his stay in the area of the 72nd Battalion, he forwarded that information to the chief of the military crime police at the MP administration in Zadar, Captain Eljuga. It was done in a way that Mr. Glavan would gather all information from all establishment units within the area. Therefore, that was certainly the information that was sent on. I apologise. As far as I can see, this is report of the chief of the military crime police at the MP administration. Based on that information he received from the field, he drafted the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just turn the page, turn one page, please. You mentioned these interviews were taking place at the reception centres at Zadar, Sibenik, and Knin, were they also taking place at the reception centre in Sinj, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I failed to mention that. There was a reception centre in Sinj in the IPK facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 65 be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit D1535, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me show you another document. This is Mr. Lausic's report to Minister Susak dated 3 December 1995. It is 65 ter 1D938.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could just take a look at the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see there the date and the fact that this is now sent to the minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in English, please. He's actually reporting on the results of the policing of the liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia in Operation Storm. And you see that he is talking now here in the middle of the page, the reporting period for him is 1 August until 30 October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, if we could turn the page in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The reporting period is 1 August until 30 October and he provides a report of all of the activities in the liberated areas: 1.576 paramilitaries were received, criminally processed, and transferred to the holding centres of the RH MUP. In paragraph 3, he reports on repressive measures taken against members of the Croatian Army by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He reports on the number of disciplinary measures filed by the military police against HV members, the types of equipment and livestock that was seized. Paragraph 4 is the section on the military crime police. And he reports that the military crime police filed a total of 201 criminal reports against 228 perpetrates for 222 crimes. Seventeen of the perpetrators were civilians and the rest were HV members. And then he breaks down the categories of crimes: 103 cases of aggravated theft, 23 cases of theft. The paragraph below is where Mr. Lausic discusses the investigations of burnings. I wanted to draw your attention to this paragraph. Mr. Lausic reports to Minister Susak that: "The investigation is being done in cooperation with the crime police of the RH MUP. We are carrying out criminal processing of 15 cases of torched residential buildings and five cases of planting explosives, for which there are reasonable grounds to suspect that the perpetrator was a HV member. The rest of the 1100 reported cases of torching and planting explosives are being processed by the RH MUP, and so far, 1069 reports have been filed for the crime of torching, and 844 reports for thefts against civilian perpetrators." Now at that paragraph can you explain to us where the RH MUP would be investigating 1100 reported cases of torching and planting explosives while the crime police of the military police in cooperation with the crime police of the military police, in cooperation with the crime police of the RH MUP is only carrying out criminal processing of 15 cases of torching. Why is the MUP carrying out 1100 investigations and you, or I should say, the crime police of the military police only involved in 15 cases?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Employees of the civilian police, when they intervene and carry out any scene-of-crime investigation or process a crime, they have to receive a report from either a civilian or their police patrols. That report should contain information to the effect that there was suspicion that a civilian committed the crime involved. Once it is reported to the competent police administration or police station, it is acted upon. That is the first initial piece of information required for the civilian police to visit a scene. The operational office of the military police or the military police battalion in that area can intervene upon being informed by either the patrol on duty, or by the civilian police, to the effect that there are reasons to believe that a member of the armed forces carried out an act of torching a residential building or a house. This makes me conclude that it was mostly the civilian police who received reports that the houses and facilities involved were set on fire by people for whom it was not established beyond any doubt that they belonged to the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the point I want to discuss with you, Mr. Milas. Why is it important to establish beyond any doubt that a perpetrator -- a suspect belonged to the Croatian Army? Why is that issue important in relationship to who is conducting the investigation of burning?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important for the reasons of competence, material competence of the courts. The military police acts only in cases which fall under the competence of the military courts. If a crime was committed by a member of the HV, the competence of the military court is not in dispute, and, therefore, the military police has to act as well. If that is not established, then the military court is not competent in material or geographical terms to act. This is regulated by the rules of work of the military police - I think Article 54 - where the Crime Prevention Service is referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, this depends on the jurisdiction of the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If it has not been established beyond any doubt that the suspect belonged to the Croatian Army, who has jurisdiction to conduct the investigation in that situation?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: An investigation in such a situation is carried out by the civilian police. They can ask additional checks to be made by the military police, to truly distinguish whether the suspect is a member of the HV or not. In case that person is not a member of the HV, the members of the police station and their senior instance, police administration that is in charge in terms of territory, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the issue of murders -- I'm sorry. It should be the previous page in the Croatian, I apologise. At the bottom. In the context of murders, General Lausic reports 41 crimes have been registered, 25 of which have been resolved, including multiple murders in Varivode, nine individuals and Gorsic, I believe that should be Gosic, seven individuals, and Zrmanja three individuals. Only two of the discovered perpetrators are members of the Croatian Army. Now as of the 3rd of December, when Mr. Lausic filed this report, did you, as chief of the Crime Prevention Service, have any information that members of the Croatian Army had committed murder in the liberated territory, other than the two referenced by Mr. Lausic in this report?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information. When the operational action Varivode was carried out, there was a certain number of people for whom it was established that they were civilians and linked with certain crimes of murder. I think that these two people mentioned by General Lausic were military personnel who were processed for those crimes, and it was determined that they had committed the murders in the general area of Kistanje or Varivode. Beyond any doubt, this has to do with establishing responsibility for the crimes referred to and that it was found out that they -- the persons involved were civilians, since they were processed by the civilian police. As for the two cases, I think it was the operational action of Varivode that resulted in the information to the effect that they were military personnel. This was done by the military police. Some weapons were seized and sent for ballistic expertise, and it was subsequently determined that one of the weapons was, indeed, used in the crime in Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: General Lausic then gives his conclusion on the work of the military police. And the last portion of the last sentence is: "We have achieved great results considering the objective conditions." As of 3rd December 1995, did you have any reason to believe that Mr. Lausic or the military police administration was dissatisfied with your work?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that feeling and no one would say so in a briefing or a meeting, irrespective of whether it would be General Lausic who was head of administration or Brigadier Biskic or his deputy, and especially not by the chief of the crime military police within the administration. That would have been mentioned in the reports prior to that in terms of asking for addendums to the reports submitted, if the situation was not as described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that 65 ter 1D938 be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who could issue -- who could promote you, Mr. Milas? Who had the authority to give you a promotion?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proposals for awards, for promotions to higher ranks, so we could call all of these as award -- awarding or commending would have to go to the chief of the military -- military police administration. The chief of the military police would send a proposal to the chief --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter kindly requests that the witness repeat his answer slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In more general terms, I would like to invite you to slow down a bit your speed of speech so that the interpreters are able to follow you, Mr. Milas. And could you please repeat the -- your last answer, which was an answer to the question: Who could promote you? And we see on the screen that you started referring to proposals for awards, for promotions to higher ranks, awarding or commending. You said it would have to go up to the chief of the military police administration and he would then send the proposal where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief would actually seek the opinion of the chief of the military police administration. So, in other words, the chief of the military police administration would seek the opinion of my chief of the crime police section in Zagreb, and once he obtained that opinion and on -- on my work and my actions, he would then take further steps and request, for instance, that I be promoted to a higher rank or to be commended or awarded or to receive a decoration and so on. So it would go to the military police administration. Now why would this have to go from the chief of the department of the military police crime department? Because he was the one who was the superior to all the staff members of the military police crime investigation department within companies and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I'd like to turn your attention to 65 ter 1D2745.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an excerpt from Mr. Lausic's diary that Mr. Lausic had deleted from his diary, and which we would now like to put to this witness. If we could go to page 2 in the Croatian, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the date here is, I believe, the 16th of August, 1995. And Mr. Lausic has notes which appear to reflect as of the 16th of August, promotions for various members of the military police. And if you look at entry number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm now noticing that, I think, the translation needs to be updated because it is number 8 in the original notes or -- maybe it is 7. I guess it is 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Major Budimir -- it says Major Budimir to the rank of colonel. Now, is it -- was it your understanding that, in fact, General Lausic authorised promotions of military police personnel after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any case, he did have the authority, and I can also see under item 7 that he proposed that Major Budimir, or, rather, he requested that Major Budimir be promoted to the rank of colonel because, up until then, he had been a major, and that Major Primorac, who was the deputy to Major Budimir, be proposed for decoration, Nikola Subic Zrinski for that medal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you look at 11, it's Major Juric to the rank of colonel; and if you look at number 12, department of crime, Captain Eljuga to the rank of major; and Senior-Lieutenant Ante Glavan to the rank of captain. This is the same Mr. Glavan who was working with you during and after Operation Storm that had been sent down to the 72nd military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct it is the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections. Just for the record, I wish to mention that Witness Lausic did not delete this page, as such; in fact, he handed over the diary, relinquished it to Court, but it was not provided with the original entries that was provided to the OTP. There was no deletion, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Going have to -- I'm not sure what Ms. Mahindaratne is referring to. We never -- it was by order of court that the original was produced, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I said, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would seem if it was deleted, it not be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if something is deleted, it doesn't exist anymore, it still does exist, and that's what you wanted to draw out attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well however we wish to classify it, Mr. President, it was redacted and we intend to address the matter later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A portion that did not appear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was redacted. And that's -- Ms. Mahindaratne that would satisfy?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It was not included in the portion that was provided to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any further qualifications to be added to that, the parties may make written submissions on how to call this portion which did not appear previously. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could have that admitted into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1537.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we've asked who could promote you. If someone was dissatisfied with your work and felt that you or the crime police in the 72nd Military Police Battalion needed to be replaced or otherwise changed, who, from your knowledge, had the authority to make the necessary changes?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Changes of final -- with a final effect could have been done by the chief of the military police. He could propose it to the chief of the military police administration, and the proposal for such a thing could be submitted to the administration also by the commander of the 72nd Battalion of the military police directly to the chief of the military police administration. So this would apply to sanctions and punishments for any type of conduct that is not in keeping with the legal norms and the orders issued and which fell within the ambit of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could General Gotovina have replaced you or otherwise made changes in the Crime Prevention Service of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gotovina, in view of the duties that he performed, could not do that, because these things were actually resolved exclusively along the professional chain of command, the military police chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of reviewing your work --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D1286 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just look at the cover page. This is the minutes of a meeting in Split that was held on 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page, please, to note the persons present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As you can see in point one, General Lausic is present; in point 2, Brigadier Biskic; number 4, Major Juric; number 5, Mr. Eljuga, acting chief of the criminal military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At number 15, Colonel Budimir is present. Now, if we could now go to English page 15; Croatian page 11, please. If we could scroll to the very bottom. This is the report of Colonel Budimir. At the bottom he says: "It is being noted that there were instances of setting fires to houses in the area of" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... responsibility of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. However, after the initial four to five days, all such occurrences were prevented."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we scroll down to Major Juric's review of the 72nd Military Police Battalion at the bottom. And if we could turn the page in Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "There are no objections to the report itself."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Major Juric reviewed the work and said in the second sentence of the second paragraph: "It is his opinion that all services OVP, PVP, and the criminal military police carried out their taskings successfully and very professionally and that all of them deserved to be commended." Then Mr. Eljuga, who would have been the acting chief of the crime police administration in Zagreb at that time reviewed the work of the criminal MP and said there are no objections. All tasks were completed on time and with high degree of quality. Now, is that after Operation Storm, other than Mr. Eljuga, Major Juric, Major Budimir, and the chief and deputy chief of the military police administrations, did anybody else have responsibility for reviewing your work?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one else had the -- even the possibility to assess my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly, OA Varivode. Could you tell us very briefly what was OA Varivode?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an operative action called Varivode, which, on 6 October 1995, was filed, based on an order issued by the chief of the military police administration, and it was filed together and in cooperation with the staff or police officers of the civilian police. This had to do with the following: A few days earlier, the assistant minister for the interior, responsible for criminal investigations, Mr. Benko, requested, in a phone conversation, that Mr. Lausic provide him information as to why the military police was not participating in investigating the multiple murders in the town called Varivode. Following this, General Lausic asked the 72nd Battalion to provide a report, on the basis of which it was determined that the 72nd Battalion did not have any information as to the commission of these crimes. And following further coordination, he issued the subject matter order on the creation of a team which would conduct an investigation or the operative action Varivode, at the head of which was Colonel Kozic, the then chief of the general crime department of the military police --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The general miliary police, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Juric, the chief of the traffic police; Captain Spomenko Eljuga, the chief of the criminal military police; and I think there was another officer from the military police administration who was involved with the activities of the AT units. The operative action Varivode, the purpose of this action was to determine, through a joint effort by the civilian police and the military police, and through their joint effort to raise the activity of these two departments of the police to a higher level, in terms of patrols and higher alertness, in order to determine all the circumstances and find out who the possible perpetrators of those crimes in Varivode were; but also to resolve some other crimes, murder, that were committed in this same area. This action, I believe, the order was issued on the 6th, and I'm not sure whether this action lasted four or five days, up until the 10th or 11th. Chief Kozic was duty-bound as the head of the team to report daily reports to the chief of the military police administration, and I think that Spomenko Eljuga was responsible for the criminal aspect and the operational and forensic steps that were taken. He had to contact the chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could -- could General Lausic, if he deemed it necessary, have ordered something like Operative Action Varivode earlier than October?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the event that he information of this type available, I believe that he would have done so; or, in other words, he had the powers to do that when the activities of the military police were concerned. In any event, when there was a reason for doing so, General Lausic, as the chief, had the authority to act upon it and certainly, at the level of the Ministry of Defence, he would also inform the minister of defence of the situation and what was going on, and that there was a need to take further measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did General Gotovina have the powers to issue something like Operation Action Varivode to the military police or to order something like Operation Action Varivode?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This has to do with the military police and civilian police effort. So this was done exclusively by way of the professional chain of command, because General Lausic could coordinate, with the assistant minister of the interior in Zagreb, the initiation of such an action, for instance; and I think that this was noted in the preamble of this order, as far as I can recall, when I was informed on this by Captain Eljuga, because I also participated together with him in parts of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Milas, I'd like to show you one document, and this is 65 ter -- sorry. First let's have P407 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I intend, simply, to ask the witness some very general questions about the document, but, simply, on the basis of the fact that he is a member of the Croatian armed forces and may provide some context, however minimal to the Chamber; but I do wish to tender a document in response to the Chamber's Rule 98 bis ruling and the citation of P407 by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Milas, this is an exhibit, it is letter from General Gotovina to General Cervenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this is an -- the second-to-last paragraph, General Gotovina writes to General Cervenko: "I do not believe that I have behaved inappropriately for an officer of the Croatian Army and mainly, that my conduct and the conduct of members of the Split Military District do not conflict with the positions of the leadership of the Republic of Croatia and state policy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 1D592, please. Mr. President, this is the letter of General Cervenko to which General Gotovina was responding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I know you have not seen this document before you came to The Hague to testify. However, does this look to you like a document what was typically prepared in the Split Military District for the Croatian Army from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that you've shown me before bears all the elements of an official document sent from the Military District of Split. If you look at the upper left-hand corner, you can see which unit, which establishment unit this came from. You see that it was classified, that this was a reference number and date. On the right-hand side, we can also see the indication as to the level of confidentiality. And as far as I could see from the document, I don't have it before me right now but I did a few minutes ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This document, I'm asking you about this document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it an official document from the Main Staff of the Croatian Army, which also bears a number, class, date, level of confidentiality and the addressee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would point out, simply, for the record, at paragraph 4, that General Cervenko is complaining in the letter, and the discussion is about treatment of UNCRO personnel at patrol during checks. And then General Cervenko says that: "Such conduct is inappropriate for members of the Croatian Army, especially because they inflict enormous damage on the reputation of the HV as a whole and are in direct opposition to state policy." So, Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen several times that a lot of fuss was made about letters being signed or not being signed. This apparently is an unsigned letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it is because it is sent via Rebus, which is an encrypted message and, therefore, it's not the actual original signed document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, the witness -- the only thing the witness told us about is that this looks like a document which will now fit into the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was using the OTP's Jan Elleby's approach, which was, It looks like an UNCIVPOL document so it comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking myself exactly what we are admitting into evidence and lack of any objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we did not objection simply because this could have been bar tabled, so, as I said this witness was certainly not the conduit to get this document in through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one last set of questions. I can finish, hopefully, in the next three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. May we have Exhibit P918 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, I need very short answers from you so that we can finish in the next three minutes, please. Now, if you turn the page in the original, please, I know you've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you know who Mario Tomasovic was during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the assistant commander of the Split Military District for PD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now based on your knowledge of the Croatian military and the functioning of the Military Districts, the assistant commander for political affairs, does he write in his own name or is he writing as part of the command of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively on behalf of the command of the Military District in Split, because, as a member of the Split Military District, he cannot take individual positions. He cannot speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is -- based on your knowledge of the Croatian military system, is this warning a warning from the Military District or to the Military District? And I mean the Military District command.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subordinates, pursuant to the Law on the Service in the Armed Forces cannot warn their superiors in this manner. This is a warning that is sent to subordinate units, in order to ensure that the political activities are undertaken in the future. So this is not a warning, if that is what you referring to, to the commander of the Military District. It is only -- it only has the heading "warning," in order to show how important the contents of this document is. So this is actually sent from the Military District to the lower level units, because all of these system units have their own political affairs assistants, all the level to the company level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps before the break, I would like to seek a few more details in relation to answers you earlier gave to my questions. I asked you whether the number of 200 torched houses, whether that corresponded with your own observations. You said that you did not travel that much after the 16th of August anymore. You told us what you had seen when you went to Kistanje, between the 10th and the 12th of August. Did you ever go through Kistanje after the 10th or 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, later on. But the number of 200 mentioned is not what was my impression with regard to that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first -- I asked you whether you went back to Kistanje at a later date, and you said, Yes. Was the situation in Kistanje then changed compared to what you had seen on the 10th to the 12th, where you said that, altogether less than ten houses, five, six in the centre; and one or two elsewhere in Kistanje, were burned. Was the situation different when you went back to Kistanje at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in the sense that I could see any greater number of houses involved than I did the last time I was there. I usually went through the central part en route to Sibenik and my impression was not that there were more burned houses in the -- in the subsequent period around the 15th or the 20th. I must say though that I did not go through that area frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Now, I interrupted you when you said something about the 200 or the number not being your impression. I interrupted you there. Could you please tell me what you had on your mind when I interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that the document that was shown to me, which spoke of the 200 houses in the area of Sector South, there's something that I wanted to common upon. This was not a clear indication to me that this occurred en masse, given the size of the area. Primarily because of the reasons I just mentioned, the reason being that I would -- I would have otherwise seen a greater number of buildings that were set on fire. That, I believe, is the problem. We have Sector South and the figure of 200 houses. This was a combat area and, to me, this does not give me an impression. Well, I may be wrong, every house is important; but this, to me, did not mean to me that this occurred en masse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there are two different matters. The first is the number and the area. First question was 200 houses reported in this document as having been burned, 16th of August. I think whatever your qualification is, whether that is widespread or not widespread, I think I asked you about whether it did correspond with your own observation. And I think your answer was that it did, or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to such an extent or to such number, in which I would truly be able to observe the 200 burned houses moving through that area. I only wanted to comment on the figure of 200, having seen it in the document. I personally did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say you have not seen 200 houses being burned, even not after the 16th of August you did not observe 200 houses, altogether, whole Sector South, with clear signs of recently being torched or burned? If you just tell me what you did observe and what you did not observe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I could see, and I must say I did not move through the entire Sector South but rather in limited areas, was that there were a lot less burned houses. The 200 houses mentioned is something that is cited in the document pertaining to the entire sector and, to me, if asked to interpret, I would say that this was not a widespread phenomenon in the area. I did see some houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have said this now five times, so that message was clearly received. I'm talking about facts you observed. Your evidence is that you, yourself, did not observe a number of 200 houses, but you observed less, and apart from that, you commented on the report. One last question: Another report that was shown to you was about approximately a thousand cases of torching that were reported. You remember that the document shown the report, I think it was from December, where an overview is given. This number of approximately a thousand, I think it was 1100 or something like that. Did that surprise you not having seen many burned houses and considering that it was not a widespread occurrence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The figure is definitely as stated, but this data came from the civilian police which had access to any area or hamlet. They went there if they had any information or reports. The routes I used follow the main routes to Sibenik or via Sinj to Split, or, from Knin by Drnis to Split. I did not use all the routes used by the police administrations of Zadar, Sibenik, and Split in the area. I only used the main roads, but I have no reason to doubt the figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we're talking about a thousand, would you call that widespread for the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a sizeable figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question, however. But I asked you whether you would call that widespread since you -- you're nodding yes from what I understand. We'll have a break. I apologise for having the break so late. We'll resume at a quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has developed some thoughts on the pending application for a subpoena for Witness AG-015. My first observation would be that the order in which the Defence preferably would present its witnesses should not prevail over any potential loss of time in court. The Chamber is very concerned about what it sees to happen at this moment; that is, to contact the witness 3 years ago and then to re-contact him, apparently, on the 18th of June or -- that's what we find in the application. I could have another look at. To my mind, it's the 18th of June as the date for -- I have just let me just refer to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's a typo, Mr. President. It should be 11th of June 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'd says 2006. So see we carefully read whatever your submissions are. Well, still then it's rather late. If you expect the witness to appear two and a half weeks after that, if you have not taken a statement, then we have health problems, et cetera. That's scheduling at too short notice. The risk of not getting where you want to go is considerable here. So, therefore, the Defence is encouraged to start preparations at an earlier stage and not two and a half weeks before the witness is expected to appear, not knowing whether he has any travel documents, any doctor's visit, any surgeries still to undergo. And, therefore, as I said before, this late start of the preparations also may result in having to give up the order in which the Defence preferably would present the evidence. Second observation, is that the Chamber strongly suggests to the Defence to take more time. The risk of a failure to have the witness appear in court on 30th of June or 1st of July is considerable. Also in view of apparent medical problems, which, as we know, usually need to be verified before the Chamber is willing to order someone to board a plane not knowing what the health problems may be. So, therefore, it is strongly suggested that you take more time, more time which would also allow you to further consider testimony through videolink. I am aware, at least I was informed, that the Prosecution would oppose testimony through videolink. If you take more time, you could perhaps further explore the medical problems, because, Ms. Mahindaratne, we've seen in this letter of the 22nd of June, that there is a claim of health problems which perhaps makes it a bit -- or, Mr. Russo. Which makes it a bit early to say that under all circumstances, that you would oppose a videolink testimony. At the same time, I am aware that no full application has been made in which the inability to travel to The Hague or unwillingness for good reasons has been put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just -- perhaps there is a misunderstanding. We were simply objecting at this point that nothing has been provided. If anything is provided with regard to health concerns, we'll certainly revisit the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, therefore, if you are considering to present this evidence possibly through videolink then, of course, the next question would be whether that could still be 30th of June/1st of July. We know that at least any travel documents problems or getting the witness before the camera takes less time than to get him in The Hague. At the same time, it needs to be organised to have a videolink, which takes its time as well. So, therefore, if you would still consider a videolink, 30th of June, or 1st of July, then you have to make a full application today with all of the details so that the Prosecution is in a position to respond; but even there, also, you could consider to take more time to say, Let's do the videolink. Let's keep that possibility open, let's further inquire into any of the health problems, and then further discuss with the Prosecution whether we ask for a subpoena, 10th of July, 12th of July or a videolink at that same later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. What we will do is see if we can gather more specific information about the health condition today. If this is an legitimate basis, we will apply probably after hours tonight, and courtesy copy everyone on the motion. I don't think it's feasible that we can file something before 4.00 p.m., given that we would have to actually go and visit the witness and obtain whatever documentation he may have. Otherwise, yes, we will endeavour to reschedule him and see if we can locate another witness to fill that time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because, finally, the Chamber understands that to a certain extent that the parties can not avoid that a gap will exist, a gap will be there. Witnesses can fall ill; witnesses can have other problems. There may be other procedural issues. One witness takes a bit more time, which disenables an another witness to appear. That is all understood but up to certain limits. And here seeing that the witness was approached apparently for the first time on 11th of June, we are slowly heading for that limit. Because at a certain moment the Chamber will have to not only consider how much time was used but also how much time was not used. And again we would not easily come to such conclusions but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I don't know that this was the time, but I can tell you that it is our intention to finish our case the first or second week of September, one way or the other. So in terms how you're anticipating and scheduling and things of that nature, the only reason at this point that we are going into September is because several of our witnesses are unable to come and testify before the summer recess. But at this point, I can advise the Chamber that regardless of any time gaps that may occur between now and the summer recess, it will remain our intention to rest our case first week of September on the outside, the second week of September, just so that you are aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Misetic. I think we have sufficiently now considered that matter. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to raise one further issue with respect to the witnesses who will be coming next week. We still haven't been informed as to who will be coming when, the order of the criminals hat not been provided to us. It is necessary for us in order to prepare to determine who is going to handle these --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I did, in fact, inform Mr. Hedaraly of the actual witnesses, so that has been given to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was that done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have to go back and look at my e-mails. I think the earlier part of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Not the identification of the witnesses, the order in which they will be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was two questions. You said the identification and the order, and I am telling you that I did identify the people who were going to come. I will send that e-mail. I'll go find you what I sent to Mr. Hedaraly, because Mr. Hedaraly had been inquiring about this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again, I'm not saying that the identification wasn't made. We were told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let's stop. If Mr. Kehoe reads the transcript, at least there's a small gap in it, but he will be aware that you asked for the order; and, as far as I can see on the transcript, nothing else, and then the answer was with the identification and only upon further request, Mr. Kehoe addressed the order. May the witness be brought into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before that, if could I just take one minute. Less than a minute, Mr. President. During the break I made some inquiries, and it transpires that the OTP has sent a RFA to Croatia requesting for documentation correspondence from the HV Main Staff, you know, outward and inward, and so this -- the document D1538 that was tendered by the Defence, the last document, should have been one of the documents which should have been sent to us in response to that RFA. So we would like to inquire from the Defence what the provenance of this document is and when the Defence received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it was attached to another document that I sought, and it would have been received in the ordinary course of obtaining documents from the Croatian archives. So I recall seeing it. It took us a long time to find it because the Chamber referenced the other response letter. We searched for it and it wasn't easy to search for it, and, ultimately, it was part of a 12-page document as an attachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you are in a position to further, during next break, to give further details because you're talking about attached to another document. Of course, the Chamber has no idea, I do not know whether Ms. Mahindaratne understands all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can't on the next break. I cannot. I will have to go back to my office, which will have to be after court today and then pull the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne you will get further details soon. I do not know is that one of the requests for assistance which is still pending to some extent under the 54 bis --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it's a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a different one. Yes, just for us, our information. Then, now, no one will stop me anymore to have the witness reappear in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like it remind everybody of the need to have a pause between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, procedural problems take their time, and I again apologise that you had to wait for such a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we'll now continue. The situation, as far as the other Defence teams are concerned, still no questions, Mr. Kay; still no questions, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means, Ms. Mahindaratne, that it's your turn now. You will now be cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milas.

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I note that yesterday when Mr. Misetic asked you what your current occupation is you mentioned that you're a member of the armed forces, which is what you have -- what is noted on the cover page of your statement. Can you be a bit more specific? What is your current designation and what branch of the armed forces are you working for?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I work for the Croatian navy in Split. Its command is in the Sveti Nikola barracks in Lora, the port. I work in the navy training centre in one of its aspects or departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you didn't mention your designation. What exactly is your work designation?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Per establishment, my post is titled intelligence affairs officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Milas, you left the military police in December 1996; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIS MILAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
